voice_event.text:
He was a real man, not an idea. Ignatius wrote against people who said Jesus only seemed to be a man, and put it as hard as it can be put: Jesus was truly born, of Mary, from the line of David. He truly ate and drank. He was truly brought before Pilate, truly nailed to the cross, and truly died - not in appearance only, the way those Ignatius wrote against claimed. And Ignatius said he was truly raised, the same way we ourselves will be raised, by the same Father.

When we give thanks over the cup - the eucharistia, our own word for that thanksgiving - we call it the vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus. More than one of our own households uses those words, not only Ignatius's own. That is the shape of it for us: a real man, really killed, really raised, and now the one through whom we give thanks.

glosses.plain_meaning: The thanksgiving: the meal of bread and cup over which thanks is given. The community returns to this table again and again, to be formed once more into one body.
glosses.quick_meaning: The thanksgiving - the bread-and-cup meal at the center of the community's life; its form varied from church to church.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Is that what we call transubstantiation?' - the later word answers a question this world had not yet asked in that form. What it held is strong enough in its own words: Ignatius calls the eucharist 'the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins' - against those who denied the body's reality - and the Didache's prayers give thanks for life and knowledge. Between those two registers no single doctrine of the elements is yet settled.
false_friend: a uniform ritual with fixed prayers (the form varies community to community)

voice_event.text:
He preached, gathered followers, and was executed by Roman authority under Pilate. That much we say plainly. But we have to tell you honestly: none of us saw him ourselves. What we have is what was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord, and appointed others to carry it forward once they themselves were gone. 

In some of our households, on the day we gather, someone reads aloud what the apostles wrote down - their memoirs of him - for as long as there is time, alongside the words of the prophets before them. That is how it reached us: not by seeing, but by receiving, and passing on what was received. We should say this plainly too: none of us claims to have known an eyewitness ourselves. Even in our own time, that chain was already felt as something thinning, not something we could simply rely on.

results.message: What does the Two Ways mean?

voice_event.speaker: pahc
voice_event.text:
Two roads lie open before every person: a way of life and a way of death. Before the water, before baptism, we taught this plainly. The way of life begins with loving God, who made you, and your neighbor as yourself - and one rule of restraint: whatever you would not want done to you, do not do to another. Walking one rather than the other is a choice kept daily, not a nature settled once and for all.

This is what one of our own communities used to teach a new member before baptism. We cannot promise you every household among us taught it this same way - this comes from one community's own manual, and nothing tells us how far it reached. But the shape of it was ours: not a threat about the afterlife in the first instance, but a living fork in the road, walked after the water as much as before it.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: pahc
voice_event.text:
Because we were taught it, handed down from the apostles who had received it from the Lord himself. One of us says it directly: the apostles preached what they had been given, and appointed others to carry it forward when they were gone. That is the chain we stood in - not our own invention, but something received and passed on.

But we have to tell you honestly: none of us whose writing survives ever saw him. The people who had walked with him were already gone by our time. What replaced their direct witness was argument - letters insisting the writer stood in unbroken line with what had been handed down, bishops claiming their office carried that weight forward. This was not a settled inheritance quietly received. It was something actively, urgently claimed, precisely because the last living link was running out.

And we believed it because we kept returning to the table. When we gave thanks over the cup, we called it the vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus. The meal formed us into what we believed, again and again.
